Claim: The intrusion began on 9 July 2026 at 21:14 UTC. This is treated as the occurrence clock.
Proves: Confirms the intrusion timestamp recorded in the incident record.
Does Not Prove: It does not independently verify the intrusion start time through a second forensic source.
Alternative Considered: Using the occurrence time as the trigger clock was rejected because the occurrence clock is different from the awareness clock.
Disposition: Used only as the occurrence clock. It is not used as the clock basis for any obligation.

Claim: The SOC confirmed unauthorized access and exfiltration on 13 July 2026 at 08:35 WAT (07:35 UTC). This is the controlling awareness clock.
Proves: Confirms the awareness event and matches public-fixtures.json V1 awareness_utc exactly.
Does Not Prove: It does not establish that no earlier undocumented awareness event occurred.
Alternative Considered: Using the 11 July EDR alert as the awareness time was rejected because the alert was queued and unreviewed, and did not identify personal data or confirm access.
Disposition: Used as clock_basis='awareness_utc' for DL-001, DL-003, and DL-004.

Claim: The confirmed EU population is 620 individuals. This was calculated by deduplicating DI-001 and DI-002, which belong to the same overlap group, EU-A.
Proves: Confirms that the independently calculated EU population matches public-fixtures.json V1 eu_unique exactly.
Does Not Prove: It does not resolve whether DI-003, which contains 85 uncertain individuals in EU-B, should ultimately be included. That remains subject to backup-index reconciliation.
Alternative Considered: Adding DI-001 and DI-002 without deduplication would produce 1,240, which would double-count the same people and would not match the fixture.
Disposition: Implemented using max-per-overlap-group deduplication in breach-engine/population.py and tested in tests/test_population.py.

Claim: The confirmed California population is 530 individuals. DI-009, which contains 44 individuals in CA-B, is excluded.
Proves: Confirms that the calculated population matches public-fixtures.json V1 california_unique exactly. It also supports excluding DI-009 because confirmed_exfiltrated='no'.
Does Not Prove: It does not establish anything beyond the exclusion of that dataset from the confirmed population.
Alternative Considered: Including DI-009 was rejected based on brief.md's instruction to exclude network-disproved datasets and DI-009's own notes, which state that network evidence excludes the archive.

Report Section: Population Calculation - Defect Found and Fixed
Claim: For GDPR Article 34 (DL-002), the high-risk source row is DI-001 only, with a high-risk subset of 214 individuals. DI-002 and DI-003 contribute zero to this subset.
Exact Locator: DI-001, DI-002, and DI-003 high_risk_subset column
Proves: Confirms that the DL-002 work item correctly identifies DI-001 as its only source row.
Does Not Prove: It does not introduce any additional high-risk individuals from DI-002 or DI-003.
Alternative Considered: The original implementation used all included population rows as DL-002 sources. This was incorrect because it included rows that contributed zero to the high-risk subset.
Disposition: Corrected. A regression test was added to confirm that zero-contribution duplicates are excluded from the high-risk source rows.

Report Section: Population Calculation - Defect Found and Fixed
Claim: When the same overlap group appears in both a yes row and an uncertain row, it must not be counted twice in upper_bound_unique.
Proves: A synthetic test with a 200-person overlap group confirmed that the upper bound remains 200, rather than incorrectly increasing to 400.
Does Not Prove: This scenario does not occur in the real datainventory.csv. It was a stress test based on a hidden-fixture-style case, not a finding in the actual incident data.
Alternative Considered: A naive approach that adds all uncertain-group contributions was shown to double-count the group. This was identified through a failing test before the fix.
Disposition: Corrected, with a regression test in place.

Claim: Password hashes use Argon2id, which is a one-way hashing method and is not decryptable. This is distinct from the decryptable encrypted-export fields.
Proves: Confirms that password hashes and the application-service-credential decryptable export are different data categories with different risk characteristics.
Does Not Prove: It does not establish whether the specific Argon2id cost parameters meet current best-practice guidance, as those parameters are not stated in the source.
Alternative Considered: An earlier draft incorrectly described the password data as decryptable. That was corrected during the fact-register review.
Disposition: The correction informs the category-based trigger design for DL-004, particularly the email_password_combo category.

Claim: Under California Civil Code Section 1798.82, as amended by SB 446, relevant personal information categories include email-and-password combinations and medical information. The encryption-key or credential-acquisition condition is part of the express safe-harbor test.
SHA-256: N/A - External web source, not a static project file
Proves: Supports the interpretation that DL-004 is based on the relevant data category and is not gated by a population threshold. The population threshold applies to the AG sample-notice requirement in DL-005.
Does Not Prove: It does not establish the complete list of permitted-delay conditions under SB 446. Only the law-enforcement-request branch was confirmed and implemented.
Alternative Considered: Relying only on the paraphrase in brief.md was not enough to resolve the trigger logic. The primary statute was consulted.

Claim: DL-002, covering GDPR Article 34, is gated on encryption_key_acquired. DL-001, DL-003, DL-004, and DL-005 are not gated on that condition.
Proves: Confirms that the engine withholds the Article 34 trigger when the export key was not acquired, because the high-risk basis exists only in the encrypted patient_support dataset.
Does Not Prove: It does not independently confirm that this legal threshold is correct. The interpretation remains a documented judgment call and has not been independently confirmed by outside counsel.
Alternative Considered: The earlier approach treated DL-002 as unconditional. That was superseded after tracing the high-risk data back to the relevant datasets.

Claim: CloudHarbor's processor notice arrived on 13 July at 10:15 WAT (09:15 UTC), after Meridian's own confirmation at 07:35 UTC. It therefore cannot be the controlling awareness clock for Meridian.
Proves: Confirms that Meridian had already established awareness before receiving the processor notice.
Does Not Prove: It does not establish whether CloudHarbor met its own 24-hour contractual notice obligation, because the evidence pack gives its detection time, not its confirmation-of-impact time.
Alternative Considered: Using CloudHarbor's notice as the awareness clock was rejected.
Disposition: The rules use Meridian's own awareness_utc or a dependent clock derived from it, never the processor notice time.
